source: Baron, Mellers, Tetlock, Stone, Ungar (2014) Two Reasons to Make Aggregated Probability Forecasts More Extreme. Decision Analysis 11(2)
finding: GJP year-1 data: the best-fitting extremizing exponent a on pa/(pa+(1-p)a) was far above 1 for both mean and median aggregates, and lower for experts than non-experts. Gain in Brier was large.
numbers: Two-option questions (80; 86 in the leave-one-out note). High-expertise mean: a=2.43 (SE 0.05), Brier 0.148 vs 0.187 untransformed (-21%). High median: a=1.78, 0.160 vs 0.176 (-9%). Low-expertise mean: a=3.08, 0.139 vs 0.196 (-29%). Low median: a=2.34, 0.153 vs 0.184 (-17%). Expertise = self-rating, median split per question; daily forecasts decayed at 0.6.
limits: In-sample optimisation of one parameter on the same questions; authors call results illustrative (study in year 3). One question judged misleading was dropped. Per-question optimal a ranged from negative (surprising outcomes) to very large, so a single a is a compromise.
agent_relevance: Human exponents 1.8-3.1 are well above the sqrt(3)=1.73 cap used in G4 reasoning. They apply to independent humans with different information, not to same-model samples.

source: Baron, Mellers, Tetlock, Stone, Ungar (2014) Two Reasons to Make Aggregated Probability Forecasts More Extreme. Decision Analysis 11(2)
finding: Two reasons for extremizing. (1) Error asymmetry: on a bounded scale, symmetric noise pulls the mean toward 0.5. The median is immune to this. (2) Regression: forecasters shrink their own log-odds by a factor c because they know they miss information; aggregating pools the missing information, so a=1/c undoes it. The median optimum depends only on c; the mean-minus-median gap reveals noise.
numbers: Simulation: for the median the optimal a equals 1/c exactly. Fit error vs simulated data under 0.005 on the probability scale. Extremizing the median still helped in the data, which is what forced reason (2).
quote: we propose that judges actually attenuate their own expressions of confidence, to take into account their belief that they are missing useful information
limits: Model assumes forecasters regress optimally and errors are symmetric in log-odds; authors say they cannot know whether regression is optimal, too much or too little. Transform-then-average is said to do worse, partly because it extremizes judgments on the wrong side of 0.5.
agent_relevance: Reason (2) needs forecasters with DIFFERENT information. Samples from one model share weights and often the same retrieved context, so reason (2) is weak for them. Reason (1) (noise near the bounds) can still apply.

source: Powell, Satopaa, MacKay, Tetlock (2022 preprint) Skew-Adjusted Extremized-Mean
finding: Re-test of extremizing on the full GJP set with out-of-sample scoring: a fitted linear extremizer of the mean cut Brier by about 38%. Partial extremizing beat pushing all the way to 0 or 1, even though the mean was on the right side of 0.5 in 91% of questions.
numbers: 462 geopolitical events, about 500 forecasters each, about 20% occurred. Out-of-sample mean Brier: arithmetic mean 0.098, trimmed mean 0.084, votes 0.080, logit 0.063, extremized mean (E-mean, b about 3) 0.061, skew-adjusted E-mean 0.046.
limits: Preprint (Jan 2022). Table text was extracted from the PDF with interleaved rows; mapping read from header order and the text's 'around 40%' claim. Reported coefficients a about -1, b about 4, c about 2 are good for both datasets; authors urge re-estimation per context.
agent_relevance: Best real-data size estimate of the extremizing gain for large independent human crowds (-38%). Gains of this size should not be expected from correlated LLM samples.

source: Powell, Satopaa, MacKay, Tetlock (2022 preprint) Skew-Adjusted Extremized-Mean
finding: Second dataset: 500 general-knowledge true/false statements, about 100 forecasts each. Extremizing again helped and partial beat full. The forecasts had a strong yes (upward) bias: the fitted intercept was large negative, so debiasing and extremizing were learned together.
numbers: Half the statements true; mean forecast above 0.5 on about 75% of questions; mean on the correct side on about 75%. Optimal pure extremizing b about 4. Mean Brier: mean 0.171, E-mean 0.107, skew-adjusted 0.098 (about 10% better than E-mean). E-mean beat the plain mean on about 76% of questions.
limits: Human data. Authors suggest the yes bias came from how statements were built (true facts with negated keywords), so it is a property of the question set.
agent_relevance: Closest evidence on acquiescence x extremizing: a linear map a+b*mean fixes shift and push together. For an LLM with yes-bias, fit the intercept first or jointly, or the push amplifies the bias.

source: Satopaa, Salikhov, Tetlock, Mellers (2021/2023) Decomposing the Effects of Crowd-Wisdom Aggregators: The Bias-Information-Noise (BIN) Model
finding: On GJP data, plain averaging helps almost entirely by cutting noise. It does not fix bias toward 0.5, and the probability mean can even add bias at long horizons. Probit (log-odds style) averaging removes most of that bias with no tuning parameter. Adding forecasters (5 to 75) gives small gains, mostly noise reduction, and does not cure the pull to 0.5.
numbers: Crowds of 5-75 sampled 250 times at a 30-day horizon; untrained individuals, trained individuals, teams and superforecasters compared. Trimming or Winsorising has a negligible effect for superforecasters.
limits: Exchangeable-forecaster model; effects are decompositions of expected Brier, not new data. Supplement tables not opened.
agent_relevance: Matches our need to average in log-odds, not probability. More samples add little once noise is gone; the remaining error is bias and shared error, which averaging cannot remove.

source: Satopaa, Salikhov, Tetlock, Mellers (2021/2023) Decomposing the Effects of Crowd-Wisdom Aggregators: The Bias-Information-Noise (BIN) Model
finding: Where forecasters share information (teams, superforecasters), disagreement is mostly noise, so averaging is already near the best and extremizing/information-fusion aggregators gain little or overfit. The regularized Bayesian aggregator (RBA) overfits when the crowd is mostly team members.
numbers: For superforecasters, differences among aggregators were small and not statistically significant (supplement S3.4.1); averaging matched supervised aggregators except at short horizons. Teams have less noise than individuals.
limits: Evidence is a model fit to GJP; exact Brier gains per condition are in figures only.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G4: the more the samples share information, the less push is justified. Same-model samples are the extreme case of shared information.

source: Satopaa, Salikhov, Tetlock, Mellers (2021/2023) Decomposing the Effects of Crowd-Wisdom Aggregators: The Bias-Information-Noise (BIN) Model
finding: RBA, which extremizes the probit average away from a common prior, reduced bias mostly at long horizons and fused information mostly at short horizons. About half of its gain was noise reduction. Prediction markets extracted partial information best; statistical aggregation reduced bias and noise slightly better.
numbers: Horizons up to about 60 days. RBA was the best unsupervised aggregator overall (bars in Fig. 6); uses prior 0.5 because GJP did not collect forecasters' priors.
limits: RBA is MCMC-based and needs a prior. Recalibration may add noise at long horizons for untrained forecasters (overfitting).
agent_relevance: Switch rule: when forecasts rest on the same evidence, average; when they rest on different evidence, push. An agent could use evidence-set overlap as the switch.

source: Lichtendahl, Grushka-Cockayne, Jose, Winkler (2018 arXiv v2; Operations Research 2022) Bayesian Ensembles of Binary-Event Forecasts / Extremizing and Antiextremizing
finding: Three ML models trained on the same data (lasso, random forest, xgboost) are an analogue of correlated samples. The best Bayesian ensemble beat the plain mean and all base models only by a hair, put most weight on xgboost, and anti-extremized the mean about one time in five.
numbers: Fannie Mae (N=1,056,724, base rate 8.49%): log loss xgboost 0.2337, plain mean 0.2347, logit aggregator 0.2329, best probit ensemble 0.2327. Carvana (N=72,983, base rate 12.3%): xgboost 0.2946, mean 0.2966, logit 0.2928, ensemble 0.2925. Ensemble extremized the mean in 79.6% and 81.3% of cases; weights on xgboost 0.607 and 0.718; power parameters 40 and 9 (near linear). 10-fold CV.
limits: Not LLMs; tabular models; log loss not Brier. Plain mean was worse than the best single model in Carvana, so pooling correlated models can lose to picking the best.
agent_relevance: Correlated, same-source forecasters: little to gain from pooling, and about a fifth of cases want a pull toward the base rate. Supports a small or absent push for same-model samples.

source: Lichtendahl, Grushka-Cockayne, Jose, Winkler (2018 arXiv v2; Operations Research 2022) Bayesian Ensembles of Binary-Event Forecasts / Extremizing and Antiextremizing
finding: Published abstract (seen only in a search result): extremizing should be defined as moving away from the base rate, not from 0.5; with shared information the ensemble sometimes antiextremizes. On public datasets it antiextremizes in 18% to 73% of cases, more often when forecasts bracket the base rate. The arXiv text (opened, d08) says shared information tends to reduce the push and can attenuate the mean.
numbers: 18%-73% antiextremizing across public datasets (abstract). arXiv v2 text: shared information tends to reduce the degree of extremizing. Cites Tetlock and Gardner (2015): teams that share information well (superforecasters) gain little from extremizing.
limits: Abstract only for the OR version; the Tetlock-Gardner claim is second-hand.
agent_relevance: Anti-extremizing is a theory-backed case, not a curiosity. Define the push relative to the base rate, not 0.5.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: Technical Report (Bridgewater AIA Labs)
finding: Same-model sampling helps, and the form of the average does not matter. Ten independent forecasts beat a single forecast, with mean, trimmed mean and median nearly equal.
numbers: FB-7-21, 1,610 questions, 10 forecasts per question, Brier: simple mean 0.1140, trimmed mean 0.1142, median 0.1138, single random forecast 0.1182 (-3.6%). 50 forecasts per question were bootstrapped; returns diminish after a handful.
limits: One benchmark, one system with search. No token-matched comparison.
agent_relevance: Confirms variance reduction from a few samples. This is the gain from the mean, before any push.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: Technical Report (Bridgewater AIA Labs)
finding: Pushing the ensemble away from 0.5 helped the same-model ensemble. A fixed Platt/extremizing factor of sqrt(3) gave a larger gain than learned isotonic or OLS recalibration, and a factor learned on another benchmark transferred only partly. The largest gains came from forecasts in 0.2-0.4 and 0.6-0.8; forecasts already near 0 or 1 gain almost nothing.
numbers: FB-7-21 Brier (table extracted with garbled rows): uncorrected mean 0.1140; fixed Platt (factor sqrt3) 0.1076 (-5.6%); log-odds extremization 0.1085; Platt learned leave-one-out 0.1071; OLS 0.1097; no correction 0.1119 (ID). Learned on Halawi benchmark (OOD): Platt 0.1104, OLS 0.1134, none 0.1125. AIA optimum coefficient 2.27; superforecasters' optimum 1.72. A move 0.497 to 0.381 changes Brier by -0.102; 0.995 to 0.999 by 2.4e-5.
limits: Row-to-column mapping of the garbled table is a best reading. Single team. Platt is applied after the supervisor step; the ensemble is 10 samples from the same agent, so this IS an extremizing test on same-model samples, but with no equal-token control. Authors warn forecasts on the wrong side of 0.5 are pushed the wrong way.
agent_relevance: Evidence against a flat 'never extremize' reading of G4: with a calibrated cap near 1.7, an extremized same-model mean gained about 5%. It also shows the gain depends on the model being hedged toward 0.5 (see d13).

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: Technical Report (Bridgewater AIA Labs)
finding: Letting a model merge samples: an agentic supervisor (can search, resolves disagreements) beat the plain mean; a non-agentic LLM merge and best-of-k did not.
numbers: FB-7-21 Brier: agentic supervisor 0.1125, non-agentic supervisor 0.1168, best-of-k 0.1191, none 0.1199. Agentic supervisor top-3 rate 33.9%; best-of-k picked a bottom-3 forecast 7.2% of the time.
limits: 'None' (0.1199) is on a different base than the 0.1140 mean in Table 9; do not compare across tables. Supervisor gain (0.0074) is of the same order as the Platt gain.
agent_relevance: Model-based merging helps only when it adds new evidence (search), not when it just rewrites numbers.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: Technical Report (Bridgewater AIA Labs)
finding: AIA explains the push by an RLHF-induced hedging bias: LLMs pull forecasts toward 0.5 and shave certain events to 0.95. They say Platt scaling corrects this, and that pushes fail if the forecast is on the wrong side of 0.5.
numbers: Example: a true probability of about 0.85 attenuated to about 0.6. Appendix G.1 shows traces that shave 98% down.
limits: Mechanism is the authors' claim, supported by example traces, not a controlled test across models.
agent_relevance: For LLM samples the main reason to push is hedging bias in the model, not information diversity. That makes the factor model-specific and needs a held-out fit; the human theory does not cover it.

source: Murphy (2026) Agentic Forecasting with Structured Linguistic Beliefs (Bayesian Linguistic Forecaster, arXiv 2604.18576 v5)
finding: An independent system found only a small gain from log-odds averaging over probability averaging, and cross-validated shrinkage chose no shrinkage. An LLM-based merge in the style of AIA was worse than a plain mean.
numbers: K=5 trials of Gemini-3.1-Pro on ForecastBench, 400 questions (791 events), no crowd anchor: gains with K for the arithmetic mean, 'a small boost' for the logit mean; leave-one-question-out shrinkage selected q=1 (pure logit mean). Logit mean is robust to a failed trial (one dead trial in five costs 9 points arithmetic vs 4 logit at p=0.95).
limits: Jensen argument does not carry to logit space; the author calls the logit choice empirical, not formal. Numbers for the logit boost are in a figure only.
agent_relevance: Prefer the logit mean as the default. No evidence that dispersion-based shrinkage helps on this data.

source: Murphy (2026) Agentic Forecasting with Structured Linguistic Beliefs (Bayesian Linguistic Forecaster, arXiv 2604.18576 v5)
finding: Replication check of AIA's Platt result on another system and benchmark: no statistically resolved overall gain for the Pro backbone; small preliminary gains on Kimi K2.5. So the AIA push result is only partly reproduced.
numbers: Platt: +0.72 Brier Index (with crowd baseline) and +1.48 (without) on Kimi; hierarchical Platt +0.98 / +1.80. Gains larger without a crowd anchor. Pro: no resolved gain.
limits: Preliminary results not tabulated; calibration used record-level leave-one-out, which the author says may be optimistic. Kimi runs differ in submission failure rates, so gains are confounded.
agent_relevance: Treat a Platt/push gain as model-dependent. Fit and check it on held-out items per backbone.

source: Aitchison, Jeen, Shevlane, Day (2026) Diversity is the Strength of the AI Crowd (ICML 2026 Workshop; Mantic)
finding: Samples from strong frontier LLMs are tightly correlated, so more draws from one model add little. The best budget-5 team spread draws across four forecasters; the least replaceable member was the least correlated one, not the most accurate.
numbers: Metaculus AI Benchmark Q2 2025, N=113 binary questions, 3 samples per model per question, 5 forecasters. Best B=5 team: fine-tuned gpt-oss-120b x2, Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5, Grok 4 x1 each. Replaceability: Grok 4 about 1.7 baseline points, fine-tuned model about 0.6, GPT-5 and Gemini under 0.1 each. Mixing two frontier models gained at most about 0.6 points over the best single; adding the fine-tuned model gained about 2.7. Aggregation was a mean clipped to [0.05, 0.95].
limits: No bootstrap CIs; authors call exact magnitudes indicative. Correlation shown as Jensen-Shannon divergence of predicted probabilities, no coefficient given. Small N. No extremizing used.
agent_relevance: Answer to gap 4 in kind: between-model correlation of frontier LLM forecasts is high; value comes from decorrelated sources. For one agent: vary evidence and method, not just seeds.

source: Schroeder, Schweisthal, Mueller, Weinmann, Feuerriegel (2026) LLM-SoccerArena (arXiv 2607.24573)
finding: Seven LLM versions asked the same football question give almost the same probabilities, and averaging them gains almost nothing.
numbers: Mean pairwise correlation of home/draw/away probabilities 0.943 (range 0.903-0.984); mean pairwise JS divergence 0.00442 nats. Equal-weight ensemble Brier 0.0047 lower than the average member; beats four versions, trails three; none significant after Holm correction. Open-book access did not change the convergence (0.00432 vs 0.00452).
limits: Three-outcome sports forecasts, different model versions rather than resamples of one model. Not temperature variation.
agent_relevance: Hard number for between-model correlation. We still lack a measured error correlation across temperature or prompt variation inside one model.

source: Turtel, Wilczewski, Skotheim, Satopaa, Tetlock (2026) How Proper Scoring Rules Shape LLM Forecasting (arXiv 2608.28482)
finding: Same-model aggregation gain for a base LLM was small, and RL training that reduces per-sample error gave more than 5x sampling. Training objectives changed bias, information and noise differently, so the noise left to average away differs by model.
numbers: GPT-OSS-120B, N=965 questions. Base: single sample Brier 0.1867, median of 5 samples 0.1788 (-0.0079), pooled 0.1861. Trained on Brier reward: single 0.1655, median-of-5 0.1610 (-0.0045). Log reward: 0.1665 to 0.1627. The Brier-trained model had little noise contribution; the log-trained one a positive noise contribution.
limits: Median-of-5, not mean, no extremizing. Trained models also changed tokens per sample (370 to 2,690).
agent_relevance: A better-calibrated single pass (0.1655) beat 5 samples of the base (0.1788), though token counts differ. Aggregation gains shrink as per-sample noise drops.

source: Palley, Soll (2019) Extracting the Wisdom of Crowds When Information Is Shared. Management Science 65(5)
finding: Seen only through a search-result snippet: the e-companion says pivoting (split shared from private information) worked less well when the coin bias was near 0 or 1, a pattern that contrasts with the prediction of extremizing procedures such as Baron et al. The PDF returned 403, so no numbers.
numbers: Not available.
limits: Not opened; claim is second-hand. Gap 8 stays open for this paper.
agent_relevance: A reminder that shared-information methods and extremizing disagree near the tails.

source: Mellers et al. (2014) Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament. Psychological Science 25(5)
finding: Only abstract-level information found (search snippet): training, teaming and tracking raised accuracy; statistical aggregation is credited to companion work. The paper's own extremizing figures were not opened. Baron 2014 (d01) says extremizing was first found in that study and that its optimal a was above 1.
numbers: Not available.
limits: The escholarship PDF was not parseable. Gap 3 (percent by team size) therefore stays open; d03 gives a first-hand percent for the whole GJP set instead.
agent_relevance: None beyond d01.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) The psychology of intelligence analysis: drivers of prediction accuracy in world politics. JEP: Applied 21(1)
finding: Full text opened and searched: it reports training, teaming and tracking effects on individual accuracy but contains no extremizing analysis. So it cannot supply the missing extremizing-by-team-size number.
numbers: Search for 'extremi' found no hits; year-1 conclusion: probability training was the most effective module and teamwork the most effective interaction.
limits: Negative finding only.
agent_relevance: None.
